mcqs.question: What's the right first move when picking a conflict-resolution strategy?
options: Determine what the data represents and whether a silent overwrite is acceptable, then pick the strategy that fits
Always apply last-write-wins as the team's default
Always adopt CRDTs regardless of data shape
Escalate every conflict to a human reviewer
mcqs.explanation: The strategy should fit the data's semantics, decided case by case. Defaulting to LWW risks silent data loss on data where it matters; defaulting to CRDTs ignores that they only fit specific mergeable shapes; escalating everything to a human doesn't scale and isn't needed where automatic merging is safe.

mcqs.question: In the vector-clock example, what does it mean when neither write's vector clock dominates the other?
options: One of the writes has an invalid vector clock and should be discarded
The two writes are truly concurrent, so there's a genuine conflict to resolve
The replica with the higher counter automatically wins, no merge needed
The writes happened on the same replica and can be safely ignored
mcqs.explanation: Neither clock dominating is exactly the definition of true concurrency — neither write happened causally after the other, so there's a real conflict that needs a resolution strategy. Neither clock is invalid, there's no automatic higher-counter win here, and the writes did not originate from the same replica.

mcqs.question: What do you give up by adopting a CRDT for a piece of data?
options: The ability to ever detect that a conflict occurred
All replication entirely — CRDTs require a single-writer system
Flexibility in the data model — the data must be shaped as something a CRDT can merge, like a set or counter
Nothing — CRDTs are strictly superior to every other strategy
mcqs.explanation: CRDTs merge automatically and correctly, but only for data shaped to be mergeable — you can't bolt one onto an arbitrary schema, so adopting one constrains the data model. They don't hide conflicts, don't require single-writer systems, and aren't a free upgrade with no cost.

mcqs.question: Why is last-write-wins risky for an inventory count?
options: It requires a distributed transaction to implement
It always runs slower than vector-clock-based merging
It cannot be implemented on any NoSQL database
It silently discards one of two concurrent writes, which for a count can mean silently overselling stock
mcqs.explanation: LWW just keeps whichever write has the later timestamp and drops the other — for an inventory count, that dropped write might be the one that mattered, silently oversetting stock. It doesn't need a distributed transaction, isn't inherently slower, and runs fine on NoSQL stores.
